slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: In “The rose is red,” red is predicated of the rose by the copula is (Lesson 3).
Drop the copula and join it straight to the noun:  “a red rose.” Now red is not asserted — it limits the noun.
So a quality-word can be predicated of a noun, or attached to it directly.
Other words name no quality — they only point out or number:  this book, two apples.
Any word joined to a noun to describe, point out, or number it is an Adjective.

slides.text: An Adjective is a word used to describe or define a noun.

slides.heading: Two Kinds of Adjectives
bullets: A Descriptive Adjective describes a noun by giving it a quality:  good, white, brave, ripe.
A Definitive Adjective points out or counts a noun, without giving a quality:  this, that, two, few.
Every quality-word is descriptive; pointing-out and number words are definitive.
Most adjectives derived from proper nouns should commence with capitals; as, American cotton, French customs.

slides.heading: Practice — Descriptive or Definitive?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each adjective is descriptive (gives a quality) or definitive (points out or counts).

slides.heading: The Article
bullets: A, an, and the are definitive adjectives called Articles.
The is the Definite Article — one particular object (“the horse”); a / an, the Indefinite Article — any one of a kind (“a horse”).
A and an are different forms of the same word: a before a subvocal or aspirate, an before a vocal.
A vocal is a vowel sound; a subvocal (b, d, g …) and an aspirate (p, t, h …) are consonant sounds — so an before a vowel, a before a consonant.
The sound decides, not the letter:  an hour  ·  a university  ·  an heir  ·  a European traveler.

slides.heading: Practice — A or An?
slides.instruction: Choose a or an for each word — listen to its first sound, not just its first letter.

slides.heading: Common Mistakes with Adjectives
bullets: Some words surprise you — go by sound: a one-way street (“w” sound), an honest man (silent h), an X-ray (“eks”), a ukulele (“yoo”).
Use this / that with a singular noun, these / those with a plural: “this kind of shoe,” not “these kind.”
Say those before a noun, never them: “those puppies,” not “them puppies.”
Don’t slip an extra a into “kind of” or “sort of”: “that kind of book,” not “that kind of a book.”

slides.heading: Practice — Fix the Adjective
slides.instruction: Each sentence has an adjective or article mistake. Give the correct word.
items: A apple fell from the tree.
I saw an unicorn in the book.
We waited a hour for the bus.
I don’t like these kind of shoes.
Those type of games are boring.

slides.heading: Commas with Adjectives
bullets: When two or more adjectives describe the same noun in the same way, separate them with commas:  a cold, dreary, endless night.
Never put a comma between the last adjective and its noun:  a kind, gentle man  (no comma after gentle).
Test — coordinate adjectives can take “and” between them or be reversed:  “a cold and dreary night”;  “a dreary, cold night.”
If you can’t insert “and” or reverse them, they aren’t coordinate but cumulative — so no commas:  “a little old wooden chair” (not “a wooden old little chair”).

slides.heading: Practice — Comma or No Comma?
slides.instruction: Add a comma between coordinate adjectives (those you could join with “and”); use none between cumulative adjectives. Write each phrase correctly.

slides.heading: The Order of Cumulative Adjectives
bullets: Recall “a little old wooden chair” — cumulative adjectives can’t be reordered. They follow a fixed sequence: OSASCOMP.
Opinion · Size · Age · Shape · Color · Origin · Material · Purpose — then the noun.
“a lovely little old round red French wooden writing desk” — each adjective in its slot.
Reorder them and it sounds foreign:  “a wooden red little lovely desk.”
A strong tendency, not a strict rule.

slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: James saw the man plowing.
The words we know fall into place: James and man are nouns; saw is the verb — transitive, with man as its object.
But what is plowing? Is it describing the man like an adjective, or telling an action like a verb?
Every word should fit one part of speech — but this one seems to be two at once.
Because it partakes of the properties of two parts of speech, it is called a Participle, which means “partaking of.”

slides.text: A Participle is a word derived from a verb, and partakes of the properties of a verb, and of an adjective or a noun.
examples: James saw the man plowing.  (plowing tells what he did, and describes him)
The boy is writing.  (the action is going on)
The letter is written.  (the action is finished)
twinkling stars  (a participle used to describe)

slides.heading: The Three Participles
bullets: Present Participle — the action is going on; it ends in -ing:  loving, writing, twinkling.
Perfect Participle — the action is finished; it ends in -ed, -d, -n, -en, or -t:  loved, written, built.
Compound Participle — the action finished before the main verb; formed with having:  having learned, having been called.
A present participle can even describe like an adjective:  “twinkling stars,” “a running brook.”

slides.heading: Practice — Name the Participle (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Point out the participle in each sentence and tell its kind: present, perfect, or compound.
items: The lesson, studied carefully, was recited.
Look at Dash playing with Rose.
This note, written in haste, reached me.
Having finished the task, I will rest.

slides.heading: Practice — Name the Participle (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Point out the participle in each sentence and tell its kind: present, perfect, or compound.
items: The boy passed on, whistling as before.
The fort, situated on a high hill, was taken.
Having eaten, the dog slept by the fire.
The children ran home, shouting with joy.
The broken cup lay upon the floor.
Having been dismissed, the class hurried out.

slides.text: A Participial Noun is a word made from a verb, used as the name of an action.
examples: I like skating.  (skating names an action)
He was in danger of losing his life.
It is a noun, though it comes from a verb.

slides.heading: Practice — Participle or Participial Noun?
slides.instruction: Tell whether the -ing word names an action (participial noun) or describes (participle). Watch the pairs — the same word can do either.
items: The boy, swimming across, grew tired.
She sat by the fire, reading.
The hunters pressed on, hoping for game.

slides.heading: Participles & the 8 Parts of Speech
bullets: A participle is made from a verb — but in a sentence it settles into one of three parts of speech.
Participle (verb): does the verb’s work, telling an action:  Look at Dash playing.
Participial adjective: does the adjective’s work, describing a noun:  A rippling stream flows by the cottage.
Participial noun: does the noun’s work, naming an action:  Playing is fun.

items: Name the two kinds of adjectives.
answers: A word used to describe or define a noun.
A, an, or the — a definitive adjective that points out a noun.
Before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
A word derived from a verb, partaking of a verb and of an adjective or a noun.
A verb-made word used as the name of an action.
